newsitem.title: USA: NYC Hevesi details improvements to watershed pact.
newsitem.headline: NYC Hevesi details improvements to watershed pact.

text.p: New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi, who declined to sign off on a $2.2 billion agreement to protect the city's watershed agreement until it was improved, on Tuesday unveiled the changes he won.

The list of improvements that Hevesi said he won from the first agreemnt, which was announced with great fanfare last autumn by New York Gov George Pataki and New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani included:
--Early, public reviews by October 1999 by the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the city and the state, in order to correct errors before pollution becomes a problem.

--The EPA keeps primary responsibility for enforcing the rules for 10 years, instead of five, and it agreed the city can avoid filtration, which would cost billions of dollars, for 20 years, instead of five, if the pact works.
--Cost controls were imposed on how upstate officials spend city money.
--Provisions that penalize upstate officials for purposely breaking their promises.
--A requirement for criteria to ensure that the pact's goal of protecting the city's drinking water is met before city funds are spent on economic development in the watershed area.
--More public scrutiny of reports, meetings and records of the new Watershed Protection and Partnership Council and the Catskill Watershed Corporation.

Despite these improvements, Hevesi said serious risks remained that the pact would not succeed, noting the regulations were not changed in response to recommendations from scientists and civic groups, new sources of pollution will be allowed into streams and reservoirs, and there are "numerous exemptions" to buffer zones designed as safeguards.
Also, he listed the following concerns:
--Upstaters can sue again over regulations, even if reports show that they should be toughened, possibly triggering delays and obstruction.
--Whether city water ratepayers get the benefit of money given to watershed residents for sewage treatment and runoff prevention depends on how wisely watershed officials spend it.
--Questions about whether upstate officials will spend the money for economic development that will not hurt water quality.
--And plans to offset new pollution that would be allowed into areas that already have problems by reductions in other areas.
